content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has provided specific recommendations for the prevention and treatment of pre-eclampsia and eclampsia, which are critical conditions during pregnancy. These guidelines were accessed on September 3, 2013. The Institute of Medicine has established dietary reference intakes for essential nutrients such as vitamin C, vitamin E, selenium, and carotenoids. These recommendations are crucial for maintaining optimal health and were also accessed on September 3, 2013. Haider and Bhutta conducted a systematic review in 2012, published in the Cochrane Database, which evaluated the effects of multiple micronutrient supplementation during pregnancy. Their findings highlighted the potential benefits of such interventions on maternal and birth outcomes. Another study by Haider, Yakoob, and Bhutta in 2011, published in BMC Public Health, further explored the impact of multiple micronutrient supplementation during pregnancy. This study emphasized the importance of addressing micronutrient deficiencies to improve maternal and neonatal health outcomes. Allen, Peerson, and Olney, in a 2009 study published in the Journal of Nutrition, demonstrated that providing multiple micronutrients, rather than just two or fewer, is more effective in improving growth and other health outcomes in children and adults with micronutrient deficiencies. The WHO has also issued guidelines on nutritional care and support for patients with tuberculosis (TB). These guidelines emphasize the importance of addressing nutritional deficiencies to improve treatment outcomes and overall health in TB patients. Irlam, Visser, Rollins, and Siegfried conducted a systematic review in 2010, published in the Cochrane Database, which examined the effects of micronutrient supplementation in children and adults with HIV infection. Their findings underscored the potential benefits of such interventions in this population. Siegfried, Irlam, Visser, and Rollins, in a 2012 Cochrane review, investigated the impact of micronutrient supplementation in pregnant women with HIV infection. Their research highlighted the importance of targeted nutritional interventions during pregnancy to improve maternal and fetal health outcomes. The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), WHO, and United Nations University (UNU) convened an expert consultation in 2001 to establish human energy requirements. This report, accessed on September 3, 2013, provides critical insights into the energy needs of various populations. The WHO and FAO also collaborated on a report detailing protein and amino acid requirements in human nutrition. This document, accessed on September 3, 2013, serves as a foundational reference for understanding dietary protein needs. Rasmussen and Yaktine edited a comprehensive review on weight gain during pregnancy, reexamining existing guidelines. This resource, accessed on September 3, 2013, provides evidence-based recommendations for optimal maternal weight gain. Singh, Mynak, Kumar, Mathew, and Jindal conducted a study in 2005, published in Archives of Disease in Childhood, which examined the prevalence and risk factors for infection transmission among children in households with adults suffering from pulmonary tuberculosis. Moran-Mendoza, Marion, Elwood, Patrick, and Fitzgerald, in a 2010 study published in the International Journal of Tuberculosis and Lung Disease, identified risk factors for developing tuberculosis over a 12-year follow-up of contacts of TB cases. Topley, Maher, and Mbewe, in a 1996 study published in Archives of Disease in Childhood, investigated the transmission of tuberculosis to contacts of sputum-positive adults in Malawi. Their findings provided valuable insights into TB transmission dynamics. Downes, in a 1950 study published in the Milbank Memorial Fund Quarterly, conducted an experiment on controlling tuberculosis among African Americans. This historical study highlighted the challenges and strategies in TB control efforts. The WHO has developed guidelines for the declaration of interests for its experts, ensuring transparency and integrity in its recommendations. These guidelines were published in 2010. The WHO's STOP TB Strategy, which builds on and enhances the DOTS approach, aims to meet TB-related Millennium Development Goals. This strategy document, accessed on September 3, 2013, outlines a comprehensive framework for TB control. The Tuberculosis Coalition for Technical Assistance has established International Standards for Tuberculosis Care (ISTC), providing a benchmark for TB diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. This document was accessed on September 3, 2013. Ralph, Kelly, and Anstey, in a 2008 study published in Trends in Microbiology, explored the potential of L-arginine and vitamin D as novel adjunctive immunotherapies in tuberculosis. Their findings suggest promising avenues for enhancing TB treatment. The WHO has published a manual for physicians and health workers on the management of severe malnutrition, including the classification of malnutrition in adults using body mass index (BMI). This resource, published in 1999, provides practical guidance for addressing malnutrition. The WHO and UNICEF have jointly issued a statement on child growth standards and the identification of severe acute malnutrition in infants and children. This document, accessed on September 3, 2013, emphasizes the importance of early detection and intervention. The WHO's report on the use and interpretation of anthropometry, published by its Expert Committee, provides a comprehensive guide for assessing physical status. This resource, accessed on September 3, 2013, is essential for health professionals working in nutrition and growth monitoring. Cegielski and McMurray, in the Encyclopedia of Human Nutrition (3rd edition), discussed the nutritional management of tuberculosis. Their chapter, published in 2013, highlights the critical role of nutrition in TB care and recovery. The WHO and FAO have developed a training course on nutritional care and support for people living with HIV/AIDS. This resource, accessed on September 3, 2013, aims to equip healthcare providers with the knowledge and skills to address the nutritional needs of HIV-positive individuals. The International Union Against Tuberculosis and Lung Disease and the WHO have collaborated on a framework for the care and control of tuberculosis and diabetes. This document, accessed on September 3, 2013, underscores the importance of integrated care for these comorbid conditions. Jahnavi and Sudha, in a 2010 study published in the Singapore Medical Journal, conducted a randomized controlled trial on food supplements in patients with newly diagnosed tuberculosis and wasting. Their findings highlight the potential benefits of nutritional interventions in this population. Martins, Morris, and Kelly, in a 2009 study published in BMJ, evaluated the impact of food incentives on the completion of tuberculosis treatment in Timor-Leste. Their randomized controlled trial demonstrated the effectiveness of such incentives in improving treatment adherence. Paton, Chua, Earnest, and Chee, in a 2004 study published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, conducted a randomized controlled trial on nutritional supplementation in patients with newly diagnosed tuberculosis and wasting. Their research provides evidence for the role of nutrition in TB management. PrayGod et al., in a 2012 study published in the British Journal of Nutrition, investigated the effects of energy-protein supplementation on weight, body composition, and handgrip strength among pulmonary tuberculosis and HIV co-infected patients in Tanzania. Their findings underscore the importance of targeted nutritional support. Sudarsanam et al., in a 2011 study published in Tropical Medicine and International Health, conducted a pilot randomized trial on nutritional supplementation in patients with tuberculosis and HIV co-infection receiving directly observed short-course chemotherapy. Their research highlights the potential benefits of integrating nutrition into TB treatment protocols. Loto and Awowole, in a 2012 review published in the Journal of Pregnancy, examined tuberculosis in pregnancy. Their review provides a comprehensive overview of the challenges and management strategies for TB in pregnant women. Mehta et al., in a 2011 study published in Nutrition Journal, conducted a randomized trial on multivitamin supplementation in children with tuberculosis in Tanzania. Their findings emphasize the role of micronutrients in supporting recovery and growth in pediatric TB patients. PrayGod et al., in a 2011 study published in the Journal of Nutrition, demonstrated that daily multi-micronutrient supplementation during tuberculosis treatment increases weight and grip strength among HIV-uninfected patients in Tanzania. However, the same benefits were not observed in HIV-infected patients. Range et al., in a 2005 study published in Tropical Medicine and International Health, evaluated the effect of micronutrient supplementation on treatment outcomes in patients with pulmonary tuberculosis in Tanzania. Their randomized controlled trial provides insights into the potential benefits of such interventions. Semba et al., in a 2007 study published in the International Journal of Tuberculosis and Lung Disease, investigated the impact of micronutrient supplements on the mortality of HIV-infected adults with pulmonary tuberculosis. Their controlled clinical trial highlights the importance of addressing nutritional deficiencies in this population. Villamor et al., in a 2008 study published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases, conducted a trial on the effects of micronutrient supplementation on treatment outcomes, T cell counts, morbidity, and mortality in adults with pulmonary tuberculosis. Their findings provide valuable evidence for the role of nutrition in TB care.
